claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a single-phase, homogeneous, disordered solid solution without significant precipitates or second phases.
This CoCrFeNiTi starting state has low hardness and low strength.
The single-phase solid solution favors easy dislocation glide.
Dislocation glide encounters minimal barriers because the material lacks precipitates, second phases, and other diverse atomic-scale obstacles.
Easy dislocation glide, rather than dislocation pile-up or forest hardening, governs the low hardness and strength.
Dislocation density, slip-system activation, and possible local solute segregation mediate the deformation response.
The homogeneous lattice minimizes lattice friction and dislocation pinning.
Reduced lattice friction and pinning suppress the formation of dislocation networks and forest hardening.
Deformation is dominated by easily activated slip and early dislocation motion.
The homogeneous solid-solution material will exhibit prominent plasticity and rapid saturation of strain hardening.
Introducing nanoscale precipitates will increase hardness and strength relative to the homogeneous starting state.
The increased hardness and strength of the precipitate-containing material will result from increased dislocation pinning.
The proposed mechanism applies to near-equimolar compositions under quasi-static tensile or compressive loading at moderate temperatures.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply under severe plastic deformation or extreme temperatures that induce phase transformations.
A precipitate-containing sample and a homogeneous solid-solution control can be compared under identical tensile or compressive loading to test the mechanism.
Failure to observe lower strength, faster strain-hardening saturation, or the predicted dislocation-behavior differences in the homogeneous control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
